scenes.visual: Title card 'Three Claims in One Drought' fades in over a sun-baked, dusty island seen from the side. THE WORLD, kept for both films (16:9, warm sand-coloured background). COLOUR MAP, same in every scene and in film 2: population before selection GREY; survivors / selected parents GOLD; offspring TEAL; S is a GOLD horizontal arrow; R is a TEAL horizontal arrow; h² is a round dial with a needle, scale 0 to 1. Finches are simple dark-brown cartoon birds, not photographs. Every number shown in the dot plots is labelled 'illustrative' on screen; the plots are schematic, not the Grants' data. Equations and numbers appear only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: In 1977 a drought killed most of the finches on a small island, and the survivors had bigger beaks. Did the finches just evolve?
scenes.visual: Cartoon island under a hard sun. A flock of about 40 small dark finches; the ground cracks and the grass browns. Most finches fade to outlines and drift off; a few remain, visibly larger-beaked. Question card: 'Did the finches just evolve?'
scenes.narration: In 1977 a drought killed most of the finches on a small island, and the survivors had bigger beaks. Did the finches just evolve?

scenes.tts: The island is Daphne Major, in the Galápagos. Researchers had banded and measured nearly every medium ground finch living there. So they knew each bird's beak before the drought began.
scenes.visual: Map inset: the Galápagos, an arrow to a tiny island labelled 'Daphne Major'. A cartoon hand fits a coloured leg band on a finch, and calipers close on its beak. A tally sheet fills with rows. Label 'medium ground finch'.
scenes.narration: The island is Daphne Major, in the Galápagos. Researchers had banded and measured nearly every medium ground finch living there. So they knew each bird's beak before the drought began.

scenes.tts: Picture each bird as a dot on a line of beak depth. Shallow beaks sit on the left, deep beaks on the right. Before the drought, the whole population makes this grey cloud.
scenes.visual: A horizontal axis labelled 'beak depth (mm)' with a schematic scale, no tick numbers spoken. About 60 GREY dots stack into a bell-shaped pile. A GREY tick marks its mean, labelled 'mean before drought'. Corner label 'illustrative'.
scenes.narration: Picture each bird as a dot on a line of beak depth. Shallow beaks sit on the left, deep beaks on the right. Before the drought, the whole population makes this grey cloud.

scenes.tts: Then the drought comes. About eighty-five percent of the medium ground finches died. The survivors were not a random sample. Larger birds, especially males with larger beaks, survived best.
scenes.caption: Then the drought comes. About 85 percent of the medium ground finches died. The survivors were not a random sample. Larger birds, especially males with larger beaks, survived best.
scenes.visual: A dry wind sweeps left to right across the GREY pile. Dots fade, many from the left, fewer from the right. The remaining dots, mostly right of centre, turn GOLD. On-screen: 'about 85% died'. A small male-symbol tag appears on several large GOLD dots.
scenes.narration: Then the drought comes. About 85 percent of the medium ground finches died. The survivors were not a random sample. Larger birds, especially males with larger beaks, survived best.

scenes.tts: Why those birds? The food left on the island was mostly large, hard seeds. Something was sorting the birds, and the seeds that were left are the leading suspect.
scenes.visual: Ground panel below the plot: small soft seeds vanish; large hard seeds remain, drawn as big brown ovals. A deep-beaked cartoon finch cracks one. A faint dotted line links the seed panel to the GOLD dots, with a label 'suspect'.
scenes.narration: Why those birds? The food left on the island was mostly large, hard seeds. Something was sorting the birds, and the seeds that were left are the leading suspect.

scenes.tts: The survivors' average now sits to the right of the old average. That gap measures selection through survival. If the survivors breed about equally, it is the selection differential, called S.
scenes.visual: A GOLD tick marks the survivors' mean. A GOLD arrow runs from the GREY mean to the GOLD mean, labelled 'selection through survival'. Then a small sub-label appears: 'if survivors breed about equally: S = selection differential'.
scenes.narration: The survivors' average now sits to the right of the old average. That gap measures selection through survival. If the survivors breed about equally, it is the selection differential, called S.

scenes.tts: So is that evolution? Not yet shown. Survival tells you who lived. It cannot tell you what their chicks will look like. That depends on inheritance.
scenes.visual: A stamp 'EVOLUTION?' hovers over the GOLD dots and stays unpressed, with a small label 'not yet shown'. An empty row appears below the plot, labelled 'their chicks', with a question mark.
scenes.narration: So is that evolution? Not yet shown. Survival tells you who lived. It cannot tell you what their chicks will look like. That depends on inheritance.

scenes.tts: Narrow-sense heritability, h squared, is the share of a trait's variation due to genes whose effects add up. That is the part that makes offspring resemble their parents. It runs from zero to one, in one population and one environment.
scenes.caption: Narrow-sense heritability, h², is the share of a trait's variation due to genes whose effects add up. That is the part that makes offspring resemble their parents. It runs from 0 to 1, in one population and one environment.
scenes.visual: A round dial appears beside the plot, labelled 'h²', with a needle and a scale from 0 to 1. A small parent finch and its chick appear beside it, their beaks outlined to show a resemblance. Label: 'one population, one environment'.
scenes.narration: Narrow-sense heritability, h², is the share of a trait's variation due to genes whose effects add up. That is the part that makes offspring resemble their parents. It runs from 0 to 1, in one population and one environment.

scenes.tts: The survivors pair up and raise chicks. Suppose beak depth were not inherited at all. Where on the line would the survivors' chicks land?
scenes.visual: GOLD dots pair up with thin connecting lines; small TEAL chick dots wait above the 'their chicks' row, not yet placed. The dial needle swings to 0. Question card: 'h² = 0: where do the chicks land?'
scenes.narration: The survivors pair up and raise chicks. Suppose beak depth were not inherited at all. Where on the line would the survivors' chicks land?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. The question card holds, the TEAL dots hover. A 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: Right back under the old average, if the environment stays the same. However strong the selection, the chicks' average would not move at all.
scenes.visual: With the dial at 0, the TEAL dots drop into a pile whose mean sits directly under the GREY mean; the TEAL pile has its own spread, not a copy of the grey one. A TEAL tick sits on the GREY tick. Label: 'h² = 0, same environment: no shift in the mean'. The GOLD arrow S stays above, unchanged.
scenes.narration: Right back under the old average, if the environment stays the same. However strong the selection, the chicks' average would not move at all.

scenes.tts: Turn the dial all the way to one, and the chicks' average lands on their parents' average. For most real traits the dial sits in between. The chicks' average moves only part of the way.
scenes.visual: The needle sweeps to 1: the TEAL pile slides right to sit under the GOLD mean. Then the needle settles at a middle position: the TEAL pile slides back to sit between GREY and GOLD means. Each pile position is a computed shift equal to the dial value times the length of S.
scenes.narration: Turn the dial all the way to one, and the chicks' average lands on their parents' average. For most real traits the dial sits in between. The chicks' average moves only part of the way.

scenes.tts: That part is the response, called R. The breeder's equation says R equals h squared times S. It predicts how far the next generation's average moves.
scenes.caption: That part is the response, called R. The breeder's equation says R = h² × S. It predicts how far the next generation's average moves.
scenes.visual: A TEAL arrow runs from the GREY mean to the TEAL mean, labelled 'R = response'. Above it the GOLD arrow S. On-screen equation, built piece by piece in matching colours: 'R = h² × S'.
scenes.narration: That part is the response, called R. The breeder's equation says R = h² × S. It predicts how far the next generation's average moves.

scenes.tts: So one sentence about a drought hides three claims. Selection happened. The trait is inherited. And the offspring changed. Each claim needs its own evidence.
scenes.visual: Three lamps in a row, unlit: 'selection', 'inheritance', 'offspring changed'. They light one at a time, GOLD, then the dial colour, then TEAL, as the narrator names them.
scenes.narration: So one sentence about a drought hides three claims. Selection happened. The trait is inherited. And the offspring changed. Each claim needs its own evidence.

scenes.tts: A survival record lights the first lamp. Comparing relatives lights the second. Only measuring the next generation lights the third. To show that selection changed a trait's average, you need all three.
scenes.visual: Under each lamp an icon slides in: a tally sheet of survivors (GOLD); a parent and chick side by side (dial colour); a row of grown TEAL chicks being measured with calipers. The equation 'R = h² × S' sits above all three.
scenes.narration: A survival record lights the first lamp. Comparing relatives lights the second. Only measuring the next generation lights the third. To show that selection changed a trait's average, you need all three.

scenes.visual: End card with the Hex mascot. Take-home line: 'Selection, inheritance, changed offspring: each claim needs its own evidence.'
